newsitem.title: UK: "English Patient" highlights UK films' cash needs.
newsitem.headline: "English Patient" highlights UK films' cash needs.

text.p: Nine Hollywood Oscars for "The English Patient" on Tuesday gave Britain's film industry a much needed shot in the arm but it still needs more cash for a full recovery.

"Once again, the Oscars have acknowledged the crucial contribution that British talent makes to films that are eventually seen by millions around the globe," British Film Institute director Wilf Stevenson said.
The media hailed the nine-Oscar haul as a sure sign that Britain's movie industry was getting back on its feet after years of suffering from a chronic lack of financing.
But some quibbled about the film's nationality.

Although it was directed by Briton Anthony Minghella and starred British actors Ralph Fiennes and Kristin Scott Thomas, "The English Patient" got its financial lifeblood from U.S. distributor Miramax, part of Walt Disney Co.

"'The English Patient' is a bit of a problem because technically it isn't a British film. Basically, it was made with Miramax. It couldn't have been made without American money," a spokeswoman for the British Film Institute said.
"But it is good news for the British film industry because it is a film that has a very heavy creative and cultural content that is British," she added.

The wealth of Oscars for "The English Patient" and five nominations for Mike Leigh's "Secrets and Lies" came at a time when Britain's film industry is enjoying record levels of investment, attendance and movie production.
Investment in Britain's movie industry surged to an all-time high of 655 million pounds ($1.06 billion) in 1996 from 394 million the previous year, according to industry figures.
Meanwhile, the number of films made in Britain jumped to 121 last year from 73.
But only 53 of last year's films were fully-funded from British sources. Many were Hollywood productions attracted by Britain's superb technical facilities.
The Arts Council of England planned to help remedy this lack of local funds by awarding 160 million pounds ($258.6 million) of national lottery funding to film groups in May.

"There is a cultural renaissance in Britain today. Our film industry is rightfully celebrated around the world. Britain truly is the media enterprise centre of Europe," said Arts Minister Virginia Bottomley.
The added cash promised to boost Britain's independent film makers. Many have accused the government of failing to give the industry enough financial support.

"I think what is important is that out there in the world we are making independent films. They're not getting interference from executives, idiots and boneheads, and that's what is important," said Mike Leigh, director of "Secrets and Lies."
